title: Cost cap introduced
description: First FIA Financial Regulations for F1 teams. Article 2.3: base cap USD 145,000,000 for 21 races, plus or minus USD 1,200,000 per race above or below 21. 2021 had 22 races, so the applicable cap was USD 146,200,000. Article 3.1 excludes driver pay (3.1(b)), the three highest-paid staff (3.1(d)) and power-unit supply costs up to the regulated maximum price (3.1(n)).
source_name: FIA Formula 1 Financial Regulations 2021, Issue 8 (15 Oct 2021), Articles 2.3 and 3.1, p.4

title: Cost cap stepped down
description: Article 2.3(a): base cap USD 140,000,000 for 21 races, plus or minus USD 1,200,000 per race above or below 21. 2022 had 22 races, so the cap before indexation was USD 141,200,000. Any inflation adjustment is not stated in this document.
source_name: FIA Formula 1 Financial Regulations, Issue 13 (8 Dec 2022), Article 2.3(a), pp.3-4

title: Cost cap base 135M from 2023
description: Article 2.3: base cap USD 135,000,000 from 2023 onwards, plus or minus USD 1,800,000 per race above or below 21 (up from 1,200,000), adjusted for indexation where applicable. Races cancelled less than three months before the event count as held. 2023: 22 races held plus Imola (cancelled at short notice) gives 23, so the cap before indexation was USD 138,600,000. Unchanged in Issue 25 (31 Jul 2025), Article 2.3, p.4: 2024 and 2025 had 24 races each, so USD 140,400,000 before indexation.
source_name: FIA Formula 1 Financial Regulations, Issue 18 (6 Dec 2023), Article 2.3, pp.4-5

title: Cost cap 215M under new 2026 regulations
description: Section D, Article D4.1.2: base cap USD 215,000,000 for up to 24 races, plus USD 1,800,000 per race above 24, adjusted for indexation where applicable. 2026 has 24 races, so USD 215,000,000. The threshold changed from 21 to 24 races and the regulations were restructured, so this figure is not directly comparable with 2021-2025.
source_name: FIA 2026 F1 Regulations, Section D Financial (F1 Teams), Issue 08 (1 Oct 2026), Article D4.1, p.D8

title: 1.6L V6 turbo hybrid power units
description: Start of the hybrid power-unit era. Article 5.1.2: engine capacity must not exceed 1600cc; Article 5.1.7: six cylinders in a 90-degree V; Article 5.1.6: single turbocharger. Energy recovery units MGU-K and MGU-H defined in Articles 1.25-1.26. Cited from the first published issue (14 July 2011); these engine basics applied from 2014.
source_name: FIA 2014 Formula One Technical Regulations (14 July 2011), Articles 5.1.2, 5.1.6, 5.1.7, p.22

title: Wider cars and tyres
description: Major aerodynamic and tyre-width change. Article 3.2.2: overall width must not exceed 2000mm. Article 12.4.1: complete wheel width 370-385mm front and 455-470mm rear.
source_name: FIA 2017 Formula One Technical Regulations (30 April 2017), Articles 3.2.2 (p.11) and 12.4.1 (p.62)

title: Ground-effect technical regulations
description: Major car redesign one year after the cost cap, built around new floor rules (Article 3.5). The two changes cannot be separated with season-level data alone.
source_name: FIA 2022 Formula 1 Technical Regulations, Issue 5 (8 July 2021), Article 3.5, p.17

title: 2026 chassis and power-unit regulations
description: New chassis and power-unit rules under the restructured 2026 regulations. Driver-adjustable front and rear wings: Articles C3.10.10 and C3.11.6.
source_name: FIA 2026 F1 Regulations, Section C Technical, Issue 14 (16 Oct 2025), Articles C3.10.10 (pp.C34-C36) and C3.11.6 (pp.C39-C41)
